analysis.one_liner: Taxes at up to 100% the bonuses and stock profits bank executives take shortly before their bank fails.
analysis.headline: A bill to claw back failing-bank executives' last-minute bonuses and stock sales won 27 Democratic cosponsors, but the House Ways and Means Committee never voted on it and it died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a bank fails, the FDIC takes it over and protects depositors; the deposit insurance fund that does this is financed by banks and ultimately the public. The DEPOSIT Act would impose a 90% tax on bonuses and a 100% tax on stock-sale profits taken by executives of a failed bank in the 60 days before the FDIC stepped in, for executives making over $250,000. It directs the revenue back into the deposit insurance fund. The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and depositors, whose publicly backed deposit insurance fund is spared the cost of executive compensation at banks that collapse. Sound banks also benefit modestly, since money returned to the deposit insurance fund reduces pressure on the fees banks pay to keep it solvent.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would tax bonuses paid by an insured depository institution in the 60 days before the FDIC was appointed its conservator or receiver at an added 90% rate for executives whose adjusted gross income exceeds $250,000 [S3].
It would tax profits from executives selling their bank's stock in that same 60-day window at an added 100% rate, effectively recouping the full amount [S3].
It states the sense of Congress that the revenue raised be returned to the FDIC's Deposit Insurance Fund, the fund that covers insured deposits when banks fail [S3].

The CRS summary describes the bill as raising revenue from highly paid bank executives at failing banks closed with FDIC appointed as conservator or receiver, with revenue directed to the Deposit Insurance Fund [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Executives of failed banks who collected bonuses or sold their own bank's stock in the two months before the FDIC took it over, and who earn more than $250,000.

drawbacks.text: The tax is narrow and applies only to payments made in the 60-day window before receivership and only to executives above $250,000 in income, so it raises little money relative to the losses bank failures can impose on the insurance fund [S3].

The provision directing revenue back to the Deposit Insurance Fund is only a nonbinding 'sense of the Congress,' not an enforceable requirement, so the money could end up in the general treasury [S3].

A penalty rate approaching 100% on late-stage compensation is a blunt tool; some would argue the better remedy is ex ante rules that force banks to fund their own failures, rather than taxing executives after the fact [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted, mostly symbolic clawback: it reaches only a small group of executives and only recent payments, so it would recover little of the real cost of bank failures, but it also costs little and directly ties the penalty to self-enrichment right before collapse. Its main value is deterrence and fairness rather than revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the rest of the Congress; the committee never took it up and it expired when the term ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded on the bill: no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history for the rest of the 118th Congress [S5].
It drew 27 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no version ever passed either chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives at failed banks keep their pre-failure bonuses and stock profits untaxed beyond normal rates, and sound banks avoid no changes to how the insurance fund is financed.

for.name: Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship in the House.

for.name: 27 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from the House Democratic caucus.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after it was referred to the committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican support is recorded; the bill died in the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee without action [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would claw back 90-100% of bonuses and stock-sale profits these executives took in the two months before FDIC receivership. Their gain came at the expense of the deposit insurance fund backed by banks and, ultimately, the public [S3].

Sound banks would benefit if clawback revenue replenishes the Deposit Insurance Fund, which reduces the assessments they pay to keep it solvent, but the bill sets no new operating rules for banks themselves [S3].
